name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
blurb: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).
title: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
answer: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).

papers.why: The most cited international policy anchor for school boards. The age-13 line for independent use gives a defensible default for PreK-8 policy: teacher-mediated only below 13.
papers.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
papers.caveat: Policy guidance, not empirical evidence. Written mid-2023; model capabilities and national rules have moved since. Global framing; US state and district rules (COPPA, FERPA, state law) govern locally.
papers.finding: UNESCO global guidance. Seven regulatory steps for governments (data protection, whole-of-government AI strategy, AI ethics rules, copyright, GenAI-specific rules, capacity building, long-term review). Recommends a minimum age of 13 for independent conversations with GenAI and asks for provider age verification and parent accountability. In 2023 only about seven countries had AI training frameworks for teachers and about 15 had AI curricula. Calls for local testing, a cumulative evidence base, and a human-centred, pedagogically appropriate interaction approach.

papers.why: A four stakeholder governance model that maps almost exactly onto the book's four audiences and its human review rule, from a different national context. The sequence (developers, then administrators, then teachers, then students) supports the book's claim that leadership and governance come before classroom use. The finding that younger students are most vulnerable to overreliance supports the grade band progression in Chapters 5 and 11.
papers.title: Future of education in the era of generative artificial intelligence: Consensus among Chinese scholars on applications of ChatGPT in schools
papers.caveat: Opinion synthesis, not outcome evidence. Chinese higher education dominates the sources. Assessment redesign advice is generic. Several claims about tool capability (adaptive assessment, real time data analysis) are aspirational.
papers.finding: Review of 12 CSSCI journal articles plus interviews with 16 university scholars and five industry experts on generative AI in Chinese schools. Views range from bans (Hong Kong universities in early 2023) to embrace, with the majority favoring cautious early adoption paired with AI literacy in the curriculum. Opportunities are grouped as learning assistants (writing, research, programming), teaching assistants (materials, assessments, workload), and teacher AI and student AI collaboration. Challenges: academic integrity, decline in higher order thinking from overreliance (with compulsory education students named as most vulnerable), inaccurate responses, privacy, and black box models. Proposes the DATS framework: developers understand education needs, ensure fairness, accountability, transparency, and ethics plus explainability, and collaborate with schools; administrators train stakeholders, create guidance, redesign policies, and update programs; teachers understand the tools, set learning goals, redesign activities, and redesign assessment; students understand the tools, learn to collaborate with AI, use it for higher order thinking, and keep academic integrity. High stakes assessment should never rely on AI alone.

papers.why: AI classroom observation is not ready for teacher evaluation; at most a coaching conversation starter.
papers.title: Validating AI-generated classroom observations: Reliability, accuracy, and limits of LLM-based pedagogical judgment
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Eight LLM endpoints rated 12 primary classroom videos against certified World Bank TEACH experts (8,618 ratings). High run-to-run variability; agreement with experts moderate at best; stable models were not necessarily accurate. LLMs leaned on explicit verbal cues over contextual evidence.

papers.title: Coauthorship integrity: Reconceptualising assessment validity for the age of generative artificial intelligence
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Reframes assessment validity around co-authorship with GenAI.

papers.why: Idea for making district AI rules auditable.
papers.title: From ethical principles to executable governance: A policy-as-code framework for trustworthy AI in higher education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Policy-as-code framework turning AI ethics principles into executable governance in higher education.

papers.why: Most direct K-12 risk evidence; supports hints-not-answers and process-based assessment.
papers.title: Potential risks of generative artificial intelligence integration into K-12 education: A scoping review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Scoping review of 22 K-12 empirical GenAI studies. Risks cluster in three areas: psychological wellbeing (emotional disconnection, isolation), intellectual agency (cognitive dependency, distorted self-assessment, loss of creative authorship), and ecological (institutional readiness, unclear governance, equity, privacy). Mitigations: value process over product, use AI for hints not solutions, embed critical AI literacy.

papers.title: School-Based Online Surveillance of Youth: Systematic Search and Content Analysis of Surveillance Company Websites
papers.finding: 14 school monitoring companies: 86% monitor 24/7 outside school, 71% use AI flagging, fewer than half have human review, 2 contact police at their discretion.

papers.why: Bias depends on detector design; public tools differ from purpose-built ones.
papers.title: Detecting ChatGPT-generated essays in a large-scale writing assessment: Is there a bias against non-native English speakers?
papers.finding: Custom detectors built on GRE data showed near-perfect accuracy and no bias against non-native speakers.

papers.title: Investigating Advanced School Surveillance Practices and Disproportionality: A Systematic Review
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 31 studies: surveillance technology concentrates in schools serving poor and minoritized students; mixed effects on perceived safety.

papers.why: Detectors are unfair to English learners; never use them as sole evidence.
papers.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
papers.finding: GPT detectors frequently misclassify non-native English writing as AI-generated.

papers.why: Supports requiring AI tools to explain why they flagged or recommended something, in plain terms.
papers.title: Explanations and trust: What happens to trust when a robot partner does something unexpected?
papers.finding: 148 adults watched a robot teammate deviate from a plan. Trust dropped. Explanations of why it acted, focused on what it sensed in the environment, best limited the trust drop.

papers.why: Directly challenges a weak version of the book's human review gate. A human who only rubber-stamps AI output is not a safeguard. The design should be human decides first, AI checks second, for grades, placement, discipline, and IEP decisions.
papers.title: Algorithms as partners in crime: A lesson in ethics by design
papers.caveat: Online adult experiments with money-sharing decisions, not school staff or school decisions.
papers.finding: Three online experiments. When the human decides and the machine corrects, people behave the same as with no corrective or a human corrective. When the machine decides and the human is the corrective (the usual human-in-the-loop setup), people rarely correct bad machine decisions and instead exploit them, becoming partners in crime.

papers.title: Attitudes Toward School-Based Surveillance of Adolescents' Social Media Activity
papers.finding: Survey of young adults, parents, teachers, administrators: young adults saw less benefit and more risk; nonheterosexual and minority respondents saw higher risk.

papers.why: Cautionary case: AI assigning high-stakes grades conflicts with the book's rule that AI never decides grades alone.
papers.title: Appraisal of high-stake examinations during SARS-CoV-2 emergency with responsible and transparent AI: Evidence of fair and detrimental assessment
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Model proposal; fairness claims by authors.
papers.finding: Proposed AI grade-awarding model with SHAP explanations to replace canceled high-stakes exams in India during COVID.

papers.title: Educational data journeys: Where are we going, what are we taking and making for AI?
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Educational data journeys framework on data power, work, identities, and literacies in school improvement data flows.

papers.why: Gives district buyers questions to ask about how a tool explains itself.
papers.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Proposes XAI-ED framework with six aspects: stakeholders, benefits, explanation approaches, model classes, human-centered interfaces, and pitfalls of explanations; four case studies.

papers.why: Useful as a caution example: biometric emotion sensing in classrooms raises consent and privacy issues.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in education: Using heart rate variability (HRV) as a biomarker to assess emotions objectively
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Adults' heart rate variability used to predict happiness and sadness for a future education tool.

papers.why: Supports the human review gate theme.
papers.title: Human-centered artificial intelligence in education: Seeing the invisible through the visible
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Editorial arguing for human-centered AI: explainable, interpretable, and governed to avoid bias and inequity.

papers.title: Social Media Surveillance in Schools: Rethinking Public Health Interventions in the Digital Age
papers.finding: No evidence supports vendor claims that social media surveillance addresses student health or safety; may harm marginalized youth.

children.name: Three Federal Laws in Plain English
children.blurb: Three federal laws carry most of the load when schools protect students online: FERPA covers education records, COPPA covers the personal information of children under 13 on commercial sites and apps, and CIPA sets filtering and safety rules for schools that take federal internet discounts.

children.name: FERPA: The Records Belong to the Family
children.blurb: FERPA gives families the right to see and control their children's education records, and schools generally need written consent before sharing personal information from those records.

children.name: COPPA: Children Under 13
children.blurb: COPPA requires companies to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13, but schools can consent on parents' behalf only when the data serves a school authorized educational purpose and no commercial purpose.

children.name: CIPA: Filters, Monitoring, and Teaching Safety
children.blurb: CIPA is the federal program that ties internet discounts for schools to an internet safety policy, and it requires blocking harmful images, monitoring minors online, and teaching students about safe online behavior.

children.name: The Newer Rules: Accessibility, Deepfakes, and State Law
children.blurb: Three newer sets of rules now shape how schools handle AI: federal accessibility standards for district websites, apps and learning platforms, a federal law against publishing intimate images including AI-generated ones, and state laws that often go beyond federal requirements.

children.name: The Approved Tool List
children.blurb: An approved tool list is a written district record of which AI tools staff and students may use, together with the rules that apply to each one.

children.name: What a Data Privacy Agreement Must Say
children.blurb: A data privacy agreement is the contract that places an education company under the school's direct control, and for AI tools it must state that student data is used only to provide the service, is not used to train general AI models, is deleted when the contract ends or the school asks, and is limited to listed data fields.

children.name: The Human Review Rule
children.blurb: The Human Review Rule holds that AI may inform a decision about a child or an employee, but a named person must make the final call.

children.name: Removing Names Before Data Goes In
children.blurb: Removing names before data goes into an AI tool is the simplest and most effective privacy habit for schools.

children.name: Rules Students Can Follow
children.blurb: A district's acceptable use policy for AI works best when it is written in plain language that students and parents can follow, and when each assignment carries a clear level of allowed AI use.

children.name: Bias Audits, Accessibility Checks, and Incident Reports
children.blurb: Bias audits, accessibility checks, and incident reports are three routine reviews that keep AI tools honest as a school's use of them grows.

children.name: Eight Questions Before the Board Approves an AI Contract
children.blurb: Before a school board approves any AI contract, it should require written answers to eight practical questions that make the risks visible before money is spent.

sections.body: This section is about the privacy and safety work that sits behind every AI tool a school uses, and it treats that work as ordinary rather than dramatic. The book opens with two real situations, a Portland school board member asking why a reading assessment contract collected fields like place of birth and migrant status, and New Mexico letting districts opt out of voice recordings in a statewide reading test. Neither was a breach, the book says, but both were about a contract asking for more than the task required, and someone had to read it and push back. From there the section moves from the laws that already apply to the rules a school writes for itself, covering federal law, newer rules on accessibility, deepfakes and state privacy, and then the practical habits of approved tool lists, data privacy agreements, human review and removing names before data goes in. The book is clear that none of this needs a law degree and none of it is legal advice, and that districts should confirm their obligations with their own counsel.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What the book finds works is a signed document for each tool and a person who has actually read it, backed by an approved tool list, a data field list and a deletion term on file. What does not work is a privacy policy on the district website or a vendor's promise in a sales meeting, because neither is evidence of anything. The common failure pattern is the free tool, where a teacher uses a helpful chatbot with student work, other teachers follow, and within a year student information sits with companies the district never reviewed, with nobody meaning any harm. The rule the book holds to is the human review rule and the habit of removing names before data goes into any tool, and it points to the research it holds, including the finding that fewer than half of school monitoring companies use human review and that GPT detectors misclassify non-native English writing as AI-generated. The Thirty Day Move is to check every tool on the inventory against a signed agreement, a data field list and a deletion term, mark each one complete, in progress or stop, and send staff a one page guide to removing names.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run in two halves that mirror the chapter's own structure. The first half builds the legal picture, starting with Three Federal Laws in Plain English and then taking each one in turn through FERPA: The Records Belong to the Family, COPPA: Children Under 13, and CIPA: Filters, Monitoring, and Teaching Safety, before The Newer Rules: Accessibility, Deepfakes, and State Law brings in what has changed more recently. A teacher or parent who wants to know what the rules actually protect would go to those pages first, and a leader would use them to check the district's own footing. The second half turns to practice, and this is where a principal or board member would spend most time: The Approved Tool List and What a Data Privacy Agreement Must Say set out what evidence has to exist, The Human Review Rule and Removing Names Before Data Goes In describe the habits that keep people in the loop, and Rules Students Can Follow extends that to the classroom. Bias Audits, Accessibility Checks, and Incident Reports covers what to do when something goes wrong, and Eight Questions Before the Board Approves an AI Contract is the page a board member would take into the meeting, since it gathers the whole section into the questions the book says every parent deserves an answer to.
